implementation_notes: SemaphoreSlim is the in-process realization for modern .NET: new SemaphoreSlim(initialCount, maxCount) bounds the permits, await WaitAsync(cancellationToken) is the non-blocking acquisition for async code, Wait()/Wait(TimeSpan) serve synchronous paths, and Release(n) returns permits - throwing SemaphoreFullException when it would exceed maxCount, which is the built-in guard against over-release that a bare counter lacks. Use it whenever the resource is process-local; the kernel-backed System.Threading.Semaphore is the sibling for cross-process or named scenarios. The classic Monitor + counter construction is not needed.
pitfalls: Release() only throws SemaphoreFullException because maxCount was set; constructing SemaphoreSlim with no maxCount lets an over-release silently widen the bound.
SemaphoreSlim is IDisposable and pending WaitAsync operations hold internal state; disposing it while waiters are outstanding corrupts them.
WaitAsync continuations run on the captured context; inside synchronous locks or on a single-threaded SynchronizationContext this can deadlock, so acquire outside such sections.

variants.name: System.Threading.Semaphore (named, cross-process)
variants.idiom_name: System.Threading.Semaphore with a name and maximumCount
variants.implementation_notes: System.Threading.Semaphore is the kernel-backed, cross-process realization: the constructor takes initialCount and maximumCount (Release beyond maximumCount throws SemaphoreFullException) and an optional name, so independent processes that open the same name share one permit counter. Its WaitOne()/Release() API is synchronous, which makes it the wrong tool for high-throughput async code but the right one for inter-process bounds (a shared device, a machine-wide license, a single-writer file).
pitfalls: Named semaphores are machine-wide and persist while any handle is open; a crashed process can leave a name that a later run silently shares, so names must be owned and cleaned up deliberately.
The kernel semaphore blocks OS threads; using it in async code ties up thread-pool threads and scales poorly compared with SemaphoreSlim.
On non-Windows platforms named kernel semaphores may be unsupported; check platform support before relying on cross-process bounds in portable code.
